To find ${f}_{yx}(x,y)$ we differentiate the given first-order partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+{y}^{2})) \\  & =y\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+{y}^{2})) \\  & =-2y\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+{y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

To find ${f}_{yy}(x,y)$ we differentiate the given first-order partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{y}(x,y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+{y}^{2})) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+{y}^{2})-2{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+{y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{yx}(x,y)+{f}_{yy}(x,y) & =-2y\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+{y}^{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+{y}^{2})-2{y}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+{y}^{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x+{y}^{2})-2y(y+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x+{y}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$
